utterances.text: I lived in the town of Odzak, municipality of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a house in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you employed in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me what work did you do in Odzak until the 19th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: I was working in agricultural company Posavina in Odzak. I worked in the following -- I was a manager of the work unit of mechanisation and then for a while I was manager of a working unit, social standard, and then until April, 1992, I worked as an internal controller.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'll ask you a small number of questions and I'd like us to go through this as quickly as possible but I think it will be very useful to hear from you some information considering that you have lived in Odzak for a long time. In 1990, and that has been uncontested so far, multi-party elections were held. Can you tell me, in the town of Odzak, who won these elections in 1990?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: In the town of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I meant the municipality of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: The municipality of Odzak, it was the party of Croatian Democratic Union that won with a large majority. After that came the Party of Democratic Action, and then the Serbian democratic party. While the other parties, like the SDP or the other parties, they had relatively small number of votes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The HDZ, did it have more than a half of votes or did it have an absolute majority in the municipality of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. It had absolute majority.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in the elections of 1990 and after the results you've just referred to were achieved, who was appointed president of the municipal assembly of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: The President of the municipal assembly of Odzak was Mr. Stjepan Ivankovic, otherwise president of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was appointed Chief of Police?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Mr. Stjepan Mikic was appointed Chief of Police. He was a member of the main board or rather the municipal board of the HDZ and he was an ethnic Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm interested in one more office, and that is the President of the executive board of the municipal assembly of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: The President of the executive board of municipal assembly of Odzak was also an ethnic Croat, Jakov Terzic, member of the main board of the HDZ of the municipality of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the basis of your answers, I believe that we can conclude that all key positions in the municipality of Odzak were in the hands of ethnic Croats, members of the HDZ. Is this the right thing to say?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for other national parties that you referred to, can you tell us who was president of the SDA in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: It was Mr. Sead Delic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the newly-established government, after the elections of 1990, did this Mr. Sead Delic have a particular office?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was one of the heads of secretariat, I don't know exactly which one, within the municipal authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me now, what about the Serbian democratic party? Who was its president in the municipality of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: The President of the SDS of the municipality of Odzak was Mr. Dragomir Tesanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the elections of 1991, did he come to hold an office in the newly-established government?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was head of the land survey office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to that, but it doesn't really relate to this particular subject, I want to put a few questions to you pertaining to local communes in the territory of the municipality of Odzak and their ethnic composition. Can you tell us about the territory of the municipality of Odzak? How many local communes were predominantly populated by Croats?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: There were nine local communes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just clarify this. What does this mean in practice? I mean what is a local commune? Is that a village?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: As a rule, these were settlements but not only. For example, the town of Odzak consisted of three local communes, so it's not a rule really.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Can you enumerate them for us? What were the local communes in Odzak that were predominantly populated by Croats?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: The part called Bijele Bare, 90 per cent of the population was Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that there were nine of them. Give me the other ones.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, in which local communes was the predominant population Croat?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: You mean individually speaking?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: The village of Ada, the village of Novo Selo, the village of Gornja Dubica, the village of Vojskova.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand this, the last two. The interpreter did not understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Very slowly, the last village that is in the transcript was Gornja Dubica. So you said Ada, Novo Selo, Gornja Dubica. Could you please proceed now?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Vojskova, Osicac, Donji Svilaj, Vrbovac, Potocani, and Crna Vas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the local commune of Trnjak Zorice. What was the situation like there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, in addition to Trnjak Zorice, where there was a mixed population, both Croats and Serbs, we had three other local communes where there was a mixed population of Croats and Serbs. That was the village of Gornji Svilaj, then the town of Odzak, and part of Donja Dubica, the so-called Papucija [phoen] was within it. And in Donja Dubica, practically in the centre of town - oh, it's not a town, it's a village - there were at least some 20 houses belonging to ethnic Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just could you speak a little bit slower? So we mentioned Croat local communes. We mentioned mixed local communes. Tell me now, were there any local communes where the Serbs were the majority population?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are the following local communes: Joseva, Mirnica, Novi Grad...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. If you cannot remember everything, it's not that much of a problem. Let me just ask you one more thing. In the territory of the municipality of Odzak, where did the Muslims live?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: The Muslims only lived in the town of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I would briefly like to move on to the town of Odzak itself. Tell me, to the best of your knowledge, as regards numbers, what was the population pattern like in the town of Odzak itself? How many Serbs were there? How many Croats? How many Muslims? To the best of your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the ethnic composition of the town of Odzak was as follows: There were about 6 and a half thousand Muslims; there were about 1500 Croats; Serbs accounted for about 560.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We can conclude on the basis of this that in the town of Odzak, obviously, the major part of the population were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that we have had a picture of the municipality of Odzak painted for us, and now I would like to move on to a subject that has to do with the municipality of Odzak. Please, have you heard of the Croat Community of Bosanska Posavina? If so, tell us who you've heard this from and what did you actually hear? What is your information in this regard?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have heard about this. Sometime in the month of December, was it the 13th or 14th of December, I was with a Muslim friend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us the name of this friend of yours and what position did he hold?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was following the little dot. Yes. His name was Enver Delic. He worked as an inspector in the crime investigation service of the SUP in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, what is it that you heard sometime on the 13th or 14th of December? I'm sorry, is this 1991? Are you referring to 1991?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us now, what is this that you heard in relation to the Croat Community of Bosanska Posavina?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Enver was having coffee at my home and he told me that on the 12th of December, 1991, in Odzak, a meeting was held of the representatives of the HDZ party from the area of the municipality, or rather the municipalities of Brcko; Orasje; Samac, Bosanski Samac; Gradacac; Modrica; Tesanj; Teslic; Derventa; and Bosanski Brod. On that day, they proclaimed the Croat Community of Bosanska Posavina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You can speak a bit faster. Please don't misunderstand me, just a tiny little bit faster.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your understanding of this? What was this actually? What was this Croat Community of Bosanska Posavina? What was your own conclusion in this regard? MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, this witness's conclusions are irrelevant. I've got no objection to Mr. Lazarevic getting this witness to tell you what he knows of this organisational body, but it should be confined to that, what he knows about it, what his source of information was, not his own conclusions. Because then you don't know on what it's based.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my question was mainly targeted to the personal experience of the witness and the way he felt, being a Serb, in Odzak, what -- how did he react and what was his reaction on this information. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, that's irrelevant. He should just tell you what's going on as far as this body is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic can ask him what his -- what the witness's reaction was when he was informed about what was going on. MR. DI FAZIO: Very well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, you heard my question. How did you react to this news that the Croatian Community of Bosnian Posavina was established? What was your feeling?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: My first conclusion was, and bearing in mind the activities so far or until then in the municipality of Odzak, and considering that the Croatian people in the municipality of Odzak is the majority population, I saw that, I felt it, as an attempt to create a kind of Croatian territory within Bosnia and Herzegovina, in the territories of the municipalities that attended that meeting on the 12th of December in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Following the establishment of the Croatian Community of Bosnian Posavina, did something change in the localities populated by Croats? Were there some changes in everyday life, in the behaviour of people?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, just very briefly, I have to stress that in the villages populated by Croats, it was a daily occurrence that convoys of cars were passing, or were driving with Croatian flags, that is with the Croatian chequerboard, with loud music on the radio in the cars, and they -- there were songs that could be heard, and these were songs of nationalistic content, and these convoys of vehicles went also through Serb villages and the town of Odzak. Furthermore, in the Croatian villages, according to what I know, particularly as of January 1992, practically on one house out of ten houses, there was a flag with the Croatian chequerboard, there were large posters and framed pictures of Franjo Tudjman, Ban Jelacic, Ante Pavlic and others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we have a pretty clear picture of what the situation was like in the Croatian villages. But it seems that in the transcript, it isn't completely clear. You said Ante Pavlic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, leader Ante Pavlic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just tell us who was Ante Pavlic, just to give a clear picture to the Trial Chamber. Can you tell us why was that important, the pictures of Ante Pavlic?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Ante Pavlic was the leader of the Croatian Ustasha state. He was a close collaborator of Adolph Hitler.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that's enough. We don't want to go into details. Can you tell us now, what happened to the Serb villages at that time in the territory of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, in the Serb villages, throughout the time, as I said in one of my previous answers, after these daily convoys with the Croatian flag and so on, there was a feeling of tangible tension.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me about the situation in the town of Odzak and then we can go on to the other events that followed? What was it like in the town of Odzak where you lived?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, the actual situation in the town of Odzak, what it appeared to be like, was normal until January, let us say until January 1992, when various incidents took place, caused or provoked by Croatian extremists, and I can list them if necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Very, very briefly, if you can just list the incidents that took place, that you personally know of, and things that you have seen for yourself in Odzak sometime after January or starting from January 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: I personally know that on the 15th of January, on the tower of the Catholic church in Odzak, a machine-gun was set up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see this?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw the barrel. A neighbour of mine, a Muslim, told me because his house is right next to the Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any other things that happened in Odzak and that could not be understood as a normal, peaceful living?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Sometime in end of January, perhaps beginning of February, I don't remember exactly, in Odzak, in the hotel, there was a group of specials from the republican MUP in Sarajevo, and they were guarding the bridge on the Sava River in Bosanski Samac, and they -- their accommodation was in the hotel in Odzak. Beginning of February, end of January, they were attacked with hand grenades, with three hand grenades, they were attacked by the Croatian extremists, and their base was in the coffee bar opposite the hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment. So these were special units from Sarajevo MUP that were guarding the bridge in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they slept in the hotel in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You can tell us if there is another incident that you think is important, but also very briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, please send some information that we are being disturbed by the banging.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, you can answer. We hope that this noise will stop.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I'd like to ask the interpreter to repeat the question. Slowly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any other incidents, any events, that you think are important, that you wish to mention that happened during that time in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, I'm sorry -- also in February, a person of Serb ethnicity, a Serb, was killed. He also worked in Odzak. He was involved in karate. He was a very peaceful, quiet man. I don't recall his name because he was not originally from Odzak but from outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, you're going into the details of what was happening in Odzak, matters which do not help the defence of your client at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: When you look at your summaries for this witness, all those are not included. He is supposed to be discussing the position of Mr. Simo Zaric in Odzak from July until late August. Please stick to your summaries and also stick to the matters which help the defence of your client. I remember earlier on in the trial dealing with this. We are not interested in what other people did. We are interested in what the indictment says the accused did. So if your defending your client, you stick to what will help the defence of your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Oh yes, Your Honour, I am fully aware of my submission that was sent to the Trial Chamber, during proofing with this witness. I made some proofing notes and I gave them to the Prosecution in respect to some new information that I received from this witness during proofing. I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, even if you've given to the Prosecution, that does not give you the right to deal with matters which don't affect the defence of your client because this is a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I understand your ruling. If I could go just briefly to one more topic in respect to the Crisis Staff established in Odzak and then I will move to the events on 17th of April, if you allow me just one thing in respect to Odzak because it is related to my case because allegedly there were some negotiations between Crisis Staff of Odzak and Samac and other -- it is -- I believe that it is related to the defence of my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I think that we have discussed the subject of Odzak enough. Can you just tell me if you know whether there was a Crisis Staff that was established in Odzak, who established it? Do you know when that was and who the -- its members were? If you can tell that to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Crisis Staff, yes, it was established, it could have happened at the end of March, possibly beginning of April, 1992. I also heard this information from Mr. Delic, whom I mentioned earlier. He told me that the Crisis Staff was established, which has about 22 members, that its members were party members of HDZ and SDA, without the participation of SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And your direct knowledge, your personal direct knowledge, with regard to the existence of the Crisis Staff in Odzak, can you tell us when that happened? When was it the first time that you officially heard, you had the opportunity to hear, that there was such a thing as a Crisis Staff in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: In terms of its information, announcement, the first time I heard personally was on Saturday, 18th of April, through our local radio station in Odzak, in -- sometime in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we just now clarify some things? Can you tell us whether army appeared in Odzak? Have you seen any troops? Who did they belong to? When was that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: This is how it was: On the 16th of April, I think it was a Thursday, I personally saw people dressed in multi-coloured uniforms, in front of a cafe in the hotel -- opposite the hotel, opposite the hotel. That is at the entrance to the hotel. These people were in multi-coloured uniforms. On the left sleeve they had insignia with the letters ZNG, that means National Guard Corps from the Republic of Croatia, and on their caps, on their -- on their caps, they had the badge of the chequerboard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the very first time you saw them?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: That was on the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, on the 17th of April, you were in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you notice something unusual on that 17th in relation to the number of people who were in Odzak? Was something going on on this 17th?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is what was going on: My house is practically right by the road that leads from Odzak to Bosanski and Slavonski Brod. There was a big convoy of cars there from the early morning hours, all day, in the direction of Bosanski Brod or rather Slavonski Brod. Then at my next-door neighbour's, who was a Muslim, I noticed quite a few civilians, women, children and men, who were staying in the houses or in the yard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were these people coming from on the 17th? Where were they coming from as they came to Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: I did not understand the question or rather I did not hear it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did these people come from, to Odzak, on the 17th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: I asked my neighbours, Nihad Terzic is my next door neighbour, I said to him, Nihad, where are these people from? And he said, "They are all from Samac. They are leaving Samac."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I asked you about the Crisis Staff of Odzak, and you said that it had 22 persons on it. Can you, to the best of your recollection, list the names of some of the persons who were on the Crisis Staff in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. According to what I heard from Enver Delic, I can say some names now but not all of them because this was a long time ago. I know, according to what Enver said, that Stjepan Ivankovic was a member, Stjepan Ivankovic, Stjepan Mikic, Anto Savic, Sead Delic, and others. I don't want to give the names of the wrong people now. I simply can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, on the 18th of April, in Odzak, what happened?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of April, I have to mention that I did not go to work all of that week. For the most part I was in my home, in my yard, or in my garden. In the afternoon, around 4.00 p.m., I noticed or rather I saw, I didn't notice, I saw, my Muslim neighbours, especially women, who started to clean the basement premises in the apartment building that is right next to my house. Then they brought water, bedding, then around 5.00 p.m. a truck came and brought a lot of sand and empty jute sacks. The men then started filling the sacks with sand and putting them on the windows that provided daylight in the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's not dwell on this subject for too long. Tell us, was there some information on the 18th in relation to the evacuation of citizens of the town of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I found out from my Muslim neighbour who lived in that building that there was an order, and that it was being repeated on the local radio station in Odzak, and also that it was going through the streets of Odzak by way of this messenger service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Did you hear this on the radio, you personally?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: I heard it in the evening, sometime around 8.30 p.m., that evacuation is compulsory of women and children of all ethnic backgrounds from the town of Odzak, to the Republic of Croatia, because during the night between Saturday and Sunday, the bombing of the town of Odzak is expected by aircraft of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you pause at this point so that I could put a few questions to you in this regard? So, the evacuation of women and children of all ethnic backgrounds was ordered and they were supposed to be evacuated to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me how was this supposed to be carried out? What were the instructions that were given over the radio?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: The evacuation -- I mean the evacuation was organised by the Crisis Staff, by buses, the Centrotrans bus company from Odzak. Every street got at least one bus respectively, with the name and surname of the driver who would be driving that particular bus. The only thing was that the buses were waiting in their garages and the sign was being awaited as to when they should start carrying out their task, namely evacuating the women and children from the town of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I just have a few questions to put to you in this regard. How did the population of Odzak react on the basis of what you could see? These women and children, did they get ready? Did they leave?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Let me say straight away, they did not leave. They were getting ready, because they had bags that were probably full of their clothes or food or whatever, I don't know, they were put out and specifically in my street, they were there lined up by the fences, and that is where the bags were when I heard the Crisis Staff -- I mean I don't know exactly. It was at 8.30 p.m., but I don't know how long those bags stayed there in view of what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, at the time you lived with your wife, your mother, and your child?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they get ready to evacuate to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: I asked a neighbour, another Muslim, whether it had to be that way, did Serbs, Croats, Muslims, women and children, have to go? And he said that they had to. And then I said, and what if I don't let them? And then he answered, "Do not play with your own life. You can all get in deep trouble." So I had this brief meeting with my family members at home, and then we decided that if they had to go, and if people in uniform came, then they should go to Croatia and then if this did not have to be so then they would remain in Odzak. I buried a briefcase with all sorts of documents related to the house and then the diplomas and also my wife's university diploma, well not really university a post-secondary school, I buried all of this imperceptibly in the garden. And I said, If you return and I'm not there, the briefcase with the documents is right over here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Odzak bombed that night by the JNA, by the JNA air force?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That day there was no evacuation of women and children to Croatia, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: No. Can I go on answering?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, please do if you think --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, at 2100 hours, the siren, the air alert siren went off and we all went to the basement of that apartment building, we stayed there until 6.00 a.m. when the siren went off again meaning that the air alert was over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. On the 19th of April, you left Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, very briefly, your departure from Odzak, were there any checkpoints? Were there military people there? Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: I was getting ready to leave Odzak even earlier. However, the town of Odzak -- or rather leaving Odzaci [phoen] towards Modrica and towards the hills, I mean that exit meant -- I mean from April, there were checkpoints there, from the 5th of April. At the checkpoints, in addition to civilians, there would be at least two persons in uniform, in the uniforms of the reserve police force, and then there were also uniformed persons, other uniformed persons, with insignia of the Patriotic League, that is to say they were Muslims, and there were also persons in uniform with ZNG insignia. So it was not easy to leave Odzak. You could leave if you knew someone but some individuals were sent back to Odzak, and since I became aware of the fact that I could no longer stay on in Odzak, for the sake of my own safety and that of my family, I decided on Sunday, the 19th of April, that on that day, I would try to leave for the first time, and the last time, the town of Odzak, that is. I said to my family, be ready. Once I decided once I'm fed up, we go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we don't really have to go into every little detail of every individual hour what was going on. So you left Odzak but which way did you go? Through which exit?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: I left Odzak at 1330 hours, the family and I, in the car, if I understood your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. Now, where did you set out when you got out of Odzak itself?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: My plan was to go to Banja Luka, where my wife had relatives. At the exit out of Odzak, at the checkpoint, there was no one there except for two reserve policemen. However, in a place by the bridge on the river of Jakesica or rather the brook of Jakesica, I saw at least 300 to 400 persons who were wearing uniforms. I have to mention another thing. Just before Jakesica, I was taken over by a Mercedes, a passenger vehicle, and it went towards the bridge. I mean that vehicle crossed the bridge, but then when I came to these people who were at the bridge, they split up, in the direction of Modrica. I passed by these soldiers and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Tell us now, so you were heading to Banja Luka, but you stopped on the way. Tell us where did you stop? How come you stayed there and how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: When I passed the checkpoint or rather the entrance into the Serb villages Vranjak I stopped at the village of Kozuhe to smoke a cigarette and to come to, both my family and I, because we couldn't believe that we had gotten out of Odzak. I turned on the radio, the car radio, this was exactly at 2.00, 1400 hours, because I needed about half an hour for that. The local radio, Radio Prnjavor, because I was going to Banja Luka via Doboj, was informing passengers travellers, rather, that they should not go towards Banja Luka at that moment because in the village of Lisnja, that is behind Prnjavor towards Banja Luka, the Muslims had set up a road block there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just a moment. The village where you stopped, what's the name of that village?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Kozuhe near Doboj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to speed things up, I hope that my colleagues the Prosecutors won't mind if I put a few leading questions to you. If I lead you through this. You stayed in that village in the house of a man you knew, and you did not even go to Banja Luka. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just tell me in terms of time, how long you stayed in that village of Kozuhe?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: I stayed in the village of Kozuhe -- I mean I'm sorry, I was in the village of Kozuhe from the 17th of July -- no, the 19th of April, from the 19th of April, 1992, until the 17th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just one question. During that time while you were in Odzak until you left Odzak, can you tell me if you perhaps saw any unit or members of JNA units in Odzak or in the villages around Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war broke out in this area, that is before April, in Odzak, there were no JNA units. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, that's right, there were no units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Apart from yourself, who were with your family in the village of Kozuhe, were there any other Serbs from Odzak who had fled and were in that village or in other surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Apart from me, there were another five people who were in the village of Koprivne, that's another village, then in the village of Okucani and in the village of Vranjak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, can you tell me what happened on the 17th of July, 1992, which made you leave the village of Kozuhe?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: On the 16th, in the evening hours, we received certain information, an information from some people who were in Odzak, reliable information, that Odzak had been liberated by the Army of Republika Srpska, and because the local telephone network worked and I had telephone numbers, so we decided to hitch a lift, six of us, and either to get to our house or to get to one of the flats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you five or six refugees from Odzak set off. You decided to go and look at -- to see your houses or your flats, since you heard that the Serb army had come in to Odzak, can you tell us what happened once you arrived in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, we walked -- we went different ways, we took a -- hitched a lift with a lorry. We got to a checkpoint, a military checkpoint, there was a military police of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment. You got to the military checkpoint where there was the military police of the Army of Republika Srpska. Can you tell us, do you know which unit this was, that was there in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: They had the insignia of the 1st Krajina Corps on their sleeve, and I also heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So you arrived at the checkpoint. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: So the military policemen asked for our IDs. We showed our ID cards. They saw that they were citizens of Odzak and then we were told that -- that that was in relation to the town of Odzak, that there was military administration in the town of Odzak, that we cannot go around the town without permits, and that we should go to the police station in Odzak until the status is resolved. So basically he warned us. He said that we should go to the SUP in Odzak, which is what we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The police station is located in the city -- in the town centre?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and the municipality as well. Everything is in the centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, from the military checkpoint until you arrived at the police station in the centre, what did you see? What was your first impression when you returned to Odzak again?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as my impression was, well, I was very happy but I saw something unusual. It was a deserted town with a lot of troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any civilians except for you five or six of you who were there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: From the checkpoint until the SUP, we did not see a civilian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, you arrived at the SUP and what happened then?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: In front of the SUP, there was a gentleman, Mr. Mirko Pavic, he was in uniform of the civilian police and I knew him, I knew him personally because he comes from Novi Grad and I know that before the war, he worked in the police station in Samac. So we greeted each other, we talked to each other, we chatted, asked each other questions and Mirko asked me straight away, because there was one of our party who was from the village of Gornji Svilaj. So he said, Fellows, this is military administration here, we don't have any permits, no permits to allow you movement. Also, there is the -- there is curfew, that is in place, until 6.00 in the morning. So the best thing would be if here at the police station, you stay until this matter is resolved. But those of us who are from Odzak, we asked, Well, can we at least take it into our own hands and go on our own responsibility and go and see our houses? He said, Well, this wasn't something to be recommended but we could go but we would have to be very careful and that if a soldier stopped you, you would have to stop -- stop, and you would have to put your arms in the air, and then you have to speak to the soldier and say the reason why you're walking. And that's how it happened. I went to my house. I visited my house. My house had been broken into. There was a window that had been broken, a window pane, there was some plastic for -- that was put on the window. I looked at the balcony, and there was a Serb woman that appeared and her husband, and another Serb appeared. And I was surprised to see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, just a moment. So what you said is that in the neighbouring building, three people arrived or appeared, there was a woman, her husband, and another Serb?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anyone else from among the civilians apart from these three that you saw and that you mentioned in the town of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: No, not then, not later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, if these three people spoke to you, can you tell us what they said to you and what was -- what had been happening in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: What was said was the following, that they had been unable to leave, this married couple, they had a vehicle, a small Fiat vehicle, that had broken down unfortunately and on Sunday on the 19th they were going to leave but they couldn't so they stayed. And then this other man, he stayed because he couldn't leave Odzak. That's at least what he told me. They stayed in the apartment and this other Serb was with them, although he had an apartment somewhere else, although he was by himself. Both these two Serb men had been taken to either the police station or the military command, they were detained, they were interrogated on a daily basis, they were accused, at least that's what they told me, they were accused by the military administration, by the civilian authorities, that they were spies, and they were also beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's time for our usual break at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will take our break at continue at 1250 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gavric, now I'm not specifically interested in the fate of these two Serbs who stayed in Odzak. What I'm more interested in is how this occurred that they had stayed in Odzak after the Serb army operation started. How did it happen that they stayed behind in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: According to what they told me, the Serbian army when they came to the place called Jakesnica, Jakes, what happens was that immediately after that, it was 13-14th or 14-15, I'm not quite sure of the date, but from Odzak, started the evacuation of civilian population, of Croats and Muslims. They stayed behind in Odzak with the intention of waiting for the Army of Republika Srpska, because the last people after civilians are -- is the regular Croatian Army that left Odzak, there was a last remaining group, the so-called Vatreni Konji, these were fire horses, those were men in uniform that were checking who of the Muslim and Croatian civilians had stayed behind in Odzak most probably. But when they saw, when the so-called fire horses stayed behind, they hid in a pantry which had no windows and they had blocked the door with a bar, with a wooden bar, and they stayed in that pantry until the 16th. And on the 16th, they heard the door open and because the woman's bag had stayed on the table. This person who had looked at the ID card that was in the handbag said, Oh, this is a Serb apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you very much. What I'm interested in is the first part of your answer, which is that if I understood you correctly, there was an organised evacuation of civilians and when this evacuation was completed, it was then that the members of the Croatian Army, that is of the HVO and the fire horses, again checked if all civilians had evacuated?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I've been told by these Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And some Serbs, those three that you saw, they managed to stay in Odzak by hiding. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So while you were there those first few days in Odzak, did someone else appear from among the civilians, from any different shelters or any other places?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. By -- until the end of July, there were 13 families, 13 Milosevic families that had lived in Bijele Bare, it's a local commune near Odzak, attached to Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just one question, these 13 members of the Milosevic family, what is their ethnicity? What are they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone else appear?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. A family Ninic, husband and wife; then Jozo Gracarevic [phone], Jozo Gracarevic, I am mentioning the name so that I can recall that. Then there was Mile Rocelo [phoen] With his wife. Then there was a man called Rade Dervic. There were a couple of families, if I have to recall all of them now --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you can just answer my next question, then we don't have to go into details, so all of these civilians who appeared during those first few days that left some shelters, what is their ethnicity, of all of those civilians?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: They are Serbs, both men and women.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any Croats or Muslims appear?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So you told me that you looked at your house, that it had been broken into, robbed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then returned to the police station?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me now, during those first few days, what did life in Odzak look like? What did you do? What was happening?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: On the very same day, a question was raised because there was the commandment of the squad, who -- and there was a question raised as to where we would sleep. And I don't know with whom Mirko spoke to do with the organs of the military administration, whether we, six of us, would be sleeping in a hotel, but we had to go in an organised way. We would have to be there before 10.00, and then once we spent the night we would then in groups organised would have to get to the SUP. So on the 17th of July we slept there, and then on the 18th of July throughout the day, we stayed in front of the SUP -- we came to the SUP building in civilian clothes. On the 19th, Mirko Pavic waited for us, met us, and said that he was given approval because there was -- civilian police was lacking, we could be engaged as civilian police in the Odzak police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment. So Mirko Pavic said that those six of you who had come to Odzak, that you could become engaged in the police?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive a uniform?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: He said there were no uniforms, go to the warehouse. If there is - because it was summer, if there is a -- if you find a pair of trousers or a jacket that fits you, just put them on. So basically we found uniforms but they were not complete uniforms, for instance, there would be a trousers belonging to a winter uniform, then there would be a jacket belonging to a summer uniform, shoes --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, were you issued weapons?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how long did you stay there to work as a policeman in the station in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: As far as I recall, I think to the maximum of eight days, and I was there in that found -- uniform found in the warehouse. I worked at the police department in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So during those eight days, what did you do as a policeman in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Nothing. Because the freedom of movement wasn't resolved, there was military administration, as I've said, and the military administration had not been resolved as to how civilians would move around the town. There were no official documents, permits, and so on. So Mirko said, People, we are not going to go anywhere until our status is resolved so that we don't have some kind of accident, because there is no documents, there is no papers, you don't have a paper -- any documents to say that I'm a member of the police station, it's Mirko who had the list. So we went in an organised fashion to the -- because there was no -- not enough place for all of us to sleep in the police station, we would go to sleep in the hotel. So our biggest worry, biggest concern was water supply, because the water net or the supply network didn't work, and -- and as far as some taps, there were not very many in town and we couldn't get to some of them and there was a problem of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the witness's words?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: -- Those few days we didn't receive from the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, the interpreters didn't manage to catch everything so can you please continue your answer? You were talking about the taps. You said that one tap worked and that the others were --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Those were in those streets, downtown, in Mahalas, as Muslims said. There was one tap and there were a lot of people going for that one tap, and then further problem was bread. Fortunately there was this woman that I had mentioned, the one who had a husband, the one that I met in the house. And I told Mirko, I'm going to go there and ask this woman to bake some bread, and that's what happened. For two or three days this woman would bake some bread, I would go and fetch the bread, and this is what we would eat. We would eat that or chickens or whatever we would manage to catch so that's -- that was our nourishment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You said there was a problem with water supply, that it was also difficult to come by food. Tell me, was there any electricity?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was it like generally speaking? Was there any destruction in town as a consequence of the war?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: No. There wasn't anything visible. I did not see anything major at that point. Even then I couldn't see anything, let alone later when I could walk around town normally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the town was not destroyed?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the services that were supposed to provide for normal living in town, that is to say the power supply, the water works, et cetera, they were not operating?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: They could not operate, because how could this be done in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So these first few days, you said that you were at the police, that you didn't do anything?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what happened then and how come you stopped being a member of the police?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly, between the 25th of July and the end of July, in the afternoon hours, in the building of the former Territorial Defence, it is right by the SUP building, I noticed a group of uniformed men leaving the building, and among them I recognised Mr. Simo Zaric, then the late Rajko Dervenic. He was wearing civilian clothing. Then I knew Mr. Savo Popovic by sight and some other people. Since this is about 20 metres away from us, we who came to Odzak, we said hello to Simo, Savo, Rajko -- I mean we met Savo and said hello to Simo and Rajko, and there were some other people there in civilian clothes. Nothing was said to us, but then the next day, Mirko Pavic said to me, Ah, yesterday the military administration established some kind of a civilian military council whose president is Mr. Savo Popovic. It has 11 members, and I congratulate you because this military council appointed you commissioner for the local commune of Odzak and please go to Mr. Savo so that he will tell you what you're supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Since we are on this very important subject now, let us just put a few questions with regard to that. So you received information that the military administration established a civilian military council?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And you said that it had 11 members?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, around 11 members.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, for the Trial Chamber to get the complete picture, you were not appointed member of the civilian military council?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. The civilian military council appointed me commissioner for the local commune of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So you were appointed by the civilian military council?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let us just deal with this civilian military council briefly. You said that it had 11 members, you mentioned some of them, Savo Popovic, Simo Zaric, Rajko Dervenic. Can you tell us who the other people there were, to the best of your recollection, who the other members were?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: I remember Mico Pavic, a Serb, a salesperson from Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Mico Pavic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, let's clarify one thing because there is a similar name and surname. Mico Pavic is not the Mirko Pavic who was in the police, those are two different men?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please continue now.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Then there was Bogdan Dragojlovic. Then Jovanovic, Jovanovic from Donja Dubica. I can't remember his first name. His sister's name is Marica though. Then there was Luka Mlinarevic from the village of Mirnica. Then there was Milenko Koic from the village of Joseva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take it slowly, please, because we seem to be losing this. We lose the names in the transcript, you see. And since this is very important for us to have these names, tell me, after this gentleman from Dubica, whose sister is Marica?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us slowly what the names of the rest of them are.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Luka Mlinarevic, the village of Mirnica. Then Milenko Koic, the village of Joseva. Bogdan Dragojlovic, did his name already, the village of Novi Grad? I can't remember any more because the members changed later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This will be sufficient. So the military council appointed you as commissioner of the local commune of Odzak? What did that mean in territorial terms, the local commune of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, in fact, it continued to live like the other local communes in the territory of the municipality -- the former municipality of Odzak, like Dubica and the other local communes. It did not have the status of a municipality any more; it only had the status of a local commune under military administration in which there was a civilian-military council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Was anybody else appointed, any other commissioners? Except for you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me just mention this. In addition to myself, all the other commissioners were appointed in villages where there was a Serb population then. Novi Grad, Gornji Svilaj, Donja Dubica, Trnjak Zorice, Joseva, Mirnica, that is when all these commissioners were appointed, on that day. Not only I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry I didn't want to interrupt the witness's answer. It's just when he says that the commissioners were appointed in villages where there was a Serb population then, it's just not absolutely clear whether he was saying pre-April of 1992 or as things had developed in the municipality following the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, if my learned colleague followed the testimony of this witness, these places that he mentioned were pre-war populated by Serbs mainly, these are local communes that were populated by Serb population before the war. So it makes sense but I will clarify that. MR. DI FAZIO: I had heard that and I think that's probably what the witness was saying, but the way it was translated it wasn't absolutely clear. That's the only matter that I raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps Mr. Lazarevic can clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one thing, Mr. Gavric, a small clarification, these commissioners who were appointed in the local communes as you said, these local communes, are they the local communes where before the war there was a majority Serb population in the territory of the municipality of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Except for local communes, were there some other commissioners as well?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. The executive organ of the military administration or rather this civilian-military council appointed commissioners for all the companies in the town of Odzak, and a commissioner for the farm in Novi Grad. Also commissioners were appointed for education, then for the Red Cross, a birth and death registry clerk was appointed. I already mentioned the one for health. So that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe you have explained the situation to us. So in addition to the territories of local communes, commissioners were appointed for certain segments of social life and also for the companies that were in Odzak; is that correct, roughly?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I would like to tender one document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: This document is already given a copy of the document to the Prosecution on Friday, so they are aware of it. It's a survey of the condition of business facilities in Odzak municipality dated July 25th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gavric, please take a look at this document carefully. Please take a look at all the pages, and then I'm just going to put a few questions in relation to this document.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could you please put it next to you now on that projector next to you so that our clients would know what this is about.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they do not have this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please tell me, have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us when, under which circumstances, and how come?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: I saw this document sometime -- I mean towards the end of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Are we talking about 1992? That's what matters really?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Ah, yes. This document was shown to me by the late Rajko Dervenic. He showed it to me as a friend. He asked me about my opinion. He said, I've been given this task by the military administration, or rather that I and the members of the civilian-military council should make a survey of the condition of the companies in Odzak. So I did this together with them. I mean, since I did not tour the companies then, I saw this, and I saw this rather, which I saw now with his signature, that's the document signed by the late Rajko Dervenic. I don't know what else to say. So I saw it, Rajko showed it to me, the lake Rajko Dervenic. He compiled this with a group that consisted of the civilian-military council because they obviously had duties according to various areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The date -- MR. DI FAZIO: Just a matter of clarification, I'm not objecting, if Your Honours please. The witness said that he was asked his opinion by his friend, and who said that he had been given the -- this task by the military administration to do a survey, and the witness said, so I did this together with them. Is the witness saying that he conducted the survey together with this civilian council? I think it's important for you to know just precisely what the civilian council was doing and its method and the way it operated, in the town. The way the witness's answer comes out, it seems to imply that he liaised with them or actually did things with them in carrying out the survey as opposed to, for example, to simply reporting to them. It's important for you to know what he was doing in -- I submit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will clarify this and I am grateful to my colleague for this intervention because I really cannot follow the transcript at the same time while examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell us just one thing: Did you personally take part in compiling this document in making this survey on the condition of business facilities in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you put this question to me again? Because I heard this interpreter through the headphones at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll repeat it straight away. Did you personally take part in assessing the situation in the business facilities and in compiling this report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your knowledge regarding this document, apart from the fact that you saw it, was what your friend Rajko Dervenic told you about, that he had compiled this with some other people?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I should mention that Rajko showed it to me. I mean the document had already been finished and it was the finished document, the typed out document, that he showed me. And he said, Well, look, this is what the situation is in our economy in Odzak. That was all that had to do with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just one other detail in relation to this document. So the document is dated the 25th of July, 1992, that means that the situation of these companies in the territory of the Odzak municipality had already been surveyed and recorded before this document was compiled. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I move to admit it fully into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D49/4 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, let us come back now to you. You told us how you found out you were appointed as commissioner for the local commune of Odzak. Can you tell us what your tasks were, who assigned them to you, and you as a commissioner for the local commune of Odzak, everything that you were supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: I've already explained in my testimony how I found out that I was appointed commissioner. I went to Savo Popovic's office, which was in the TO staff, and he told me officially that I was appointed as commissioner of the Odzak local commune by the military administration, that is by the executive organ of the civilian organ of the military administration of the military council, and that my priority task and that the other tasks will be determined later, but the priority task was to carry out repairs to the water supply network. That is that the well, the water supply well, should be repaired, that is the generator should be repaired, that is supplying it with electricity. Furthermore, that the pumps that -- these are pumps of the Hungarian type with certain balls, and that these pumps should be repaired that were part of the network so that the town would have a water supply. When he told me that this was priority task, because the town was full of troops, he told me that once this is repaired, that I would have to make sure that there is a bacteriological and chemical analysis of the water at least twice a week. That was the very first task I was given by Mr. Savo Popovic, so this is repairing and putting into function the water supply network in Odzak. Later on, I had some other tasks of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll talk about this later. But before the war, you also worked in a water supply company; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I worked in the water supply company in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me now, you became commissioner. You were given tasks to repair the water supply, but of course you were not able to do this by yourself. Were you given men, in which way, when?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you straight away, when Savo told me about this problem of the water supply and told me that this was a priority task, I said, Savo, I have nobody to do this with. There is nobody who can do this because you need an electrician, you need an expert, you need a plumber who is an expert, and then you have to lower these pumps into the well, so basically you have to start the generator and the pumps. You have to make them work. And he told me, the workforce is not your problem. The next day, tomorrow, you will get repairmen, workmen who are qualified to repair the generator and the water supply network. That's what I was told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, the next day, these people who were promised to you, did they arrive?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Savo came to work early and he said, "Today you will get four repairmen who will be working on repairing the water supply network." And Mirko said, because the station had to be cleaned and some other works -- work had to be done, "Can you see what you can do regarding this?" So he said, immediately in the morning, I would get four repairmen, four plumbers, to work on repairing the water supply network, that is the generator and everything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These four repairmen, did they arrive?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Four repairmen arrived in a lorry. Together with them came the lorry driver, and another co-driver. I didn't know who he was. He turned out this was Stojan Blagojevic, who was their security, and they came together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they came in a lorry from Samac, these repairmen that you asked for, they came from Blagojevic and with another driver. Where did they come to? Where did they drive to?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: In front of the SUP building, where my office was, as well as the office of -- of the military council.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, did you know these people from before?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, did you then meet them? Who were these people? What were their names?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, I didn't meet them individually, but I knew their last names. I mean, I knew their nicknames. I heard that these were Muslims from Samac, repairmen, plumbers, who were supposed to stay in Odzak and work on the water supply network.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us these nicknames?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: There was a Franc. He's -- I know he is of Hungarian ethnicity. That was his first name. Then there was a Muslim, Ziga, a short man. That's what they called him, Ziga. Then there was a very large man with a mustache, a blond. He was probably about 120 plus kilos. He was called Dasa. And there were some others but I can't remember the nickname.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So this was this group that came to repair the water supply network in Odzak. Did they work? Who was giving them tasks? Who was telling them what assignments to carry out?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to stress something. When I noticed that these were Muslims from Samac, because I then talked to Mirko Pavic, because they were supposed to walk around, move around, Odzak, is that they should always be escorted by civilian policemen from Odzak and he should be with them at all times and also escort them to lunch, wherever lunch would be. So this is just to stress --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's clarify something. You said that when you saw that these were Muslims, and that Odzak was full of troops, what was the motive -- what was the motive to assign a policeman to this group while they were working?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, that's for their own safety, because we couldn't issue any kind of permit, any kind of freedom-of-movement permit, document, because that had not come into force yet. Even I had not received a permit for movement around the town of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, but can you tell me what's the reason?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, for their personal safety, just in case something happened, to avoid a situation where a soldier would arrive and meet them and mistreat them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think this is now clear. Can you just tell me, in relation to what they would do on a certain day on the water supply network, what were the specific tasks for that day, for the following day, who was the one giving them assignments?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, once we agreed this, the four of them and myself and the civilian military policeman, we then went to the water supply network, and I told them, "You see, men, this is what has to be done." And again, first they had a look at everything, and then they -- they managed to get the generator to start operating. Once that was switched on and that was functioning, then that's when they connected the pumps. That was the part of their expert work. They first switched on one pump and it was working, and then they switched off the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We don't need these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What is of interest is that they worked, if so they did, for how long, whether they were paid and -- the salient features according to the case against the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm really trying to stick to the relevant facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, sir, because you did not answer my question, the question that I asked, can you please tell me who was giving them assignments as to what to do?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: In Odzak, working on the water supply, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell me, first of all, how long did they work for? Did they work every day? How long was their work assignment in Odzak? How long did they stay in Odzak in order to work?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, their working day was from the time they arrived from Samac, so sometimes they arrived at 9.00, sometimes they arrived at 8.30, their working hours were until 4.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: And then they would --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just a moment. I'll ask you short questions so that we would get the answers that we need in these proceedings. Where did these people eat?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: When the organised meals started for all of us, including the civilians from the military administration, we were given approval that all of us could eat in the hotel. So we all ate in the hotel, even some from the command staff, and then there were -- the troops had their own kitchens. In the hotel, we ate, those of us who lived in Odzak and the people who were on work obligation coming from Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. So you all ate together in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Even we would get coffee and juice. So whatever I was given, they were given.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just please can you follow my question so that we don't expand too much? Was there any difference between what you were eating and what these people who were brought from Samac were eating?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Absolutely nothing, absolutely no difference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You all ate the same food in the same place?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: We all ate the same food in the same place. In fact, we even ate at the same table. That was completely normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you have any information whether these people who worked in Odzak, and I mean the people who came from Samac for their work obligation, to Odzak, did they receive money in terms of remuneration for their work they did in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: In Odzak, they did not, because nobody could pay them, but whether they received any remuneration in Samac, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you tell me now, how long did this repair of the water network last in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, the first task that was given, which was to start the water supply, that lasted a couple of days, two to three days, until that started operating. By then, work was continuous, that is the water supply network had been damaged in the entire town, because of the tank movement and the heavy vehicles, there were pipes that were broken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gavric. Can you just tell us how long did it take, was it one month, two months, these people, how long were they there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN GAVRIC
utterances.text: I think that lasted until mid-October, this group kept coming in 1992, until beginning of October, until the beginning of October 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, one question in relation to the water supply network and the work that was done. Did you on any occasion send some of the -- these repairmen who were there to Novi Grad to a cattle form to repair something that was broken?
